source.title: One axis and two features, how I solved the first puzzle from BlueDot and how a classifier hid country on the food direction

record.file_problem: None noted; the full post text is present.
record.tranche_reason: It tests whether independently labelled features share an activation direction and whether a linear probe misses information, using a text classifier and probe/geometry analyses rather than the original neuron-visualization method.
record.gate_note: The post also reports results from adversarially training encoders to hide country from a linear probe. Those results are recorded as induced behavior, not evidence that the behavior arises without that training. The pairwise Boolean-combination analysis is reported as an aggregate best match across 63 tests; the separate pair results are not reproduced here.
record.test_reason: The post never examines individual neurons. It probes a 64-dimensional activation space for feature directions and finds that a direction-level 'country' feature is nonlinearly encoded on the food direction. That is direction-level feature sharing and linear decodability, a related but different construct from neuron polysemanticity. The author also gives no neuron-level rates or counts. The superposition label is an interpretation the post does not test. There is no capacity comparison: 8 features in 64 dimensions is not obviously a capacity-pressure setting. The puzzle model was supplied by BlueDot to contain a hidden feature, so the encoding may have been built on purpose rather than having arisen naturally.
record.authors_conclusion: The paraphrase is mostly right. The author concludes that the classifier stores food and the independent country feature on one direction, read by sign and by magnitude respectively, and that linear probes can therefore miss features. The author also concludes that adversarial training can hide a feature from linear probes without erasing it. Finally, the author asserts, without testing it, that superposition arises under pressure from a dimensionality constraint.
record.recipe_differences: The post probes a text classifier's hidden activations with linear, nonlinear, and quadratic readouts and analyzes fitted geometry; it does not use the original source's image-neuron visualization method.
record.method_sensitivity: The country result changes with the readout: linear probes are near chance, while nonlinear or quadratic readouts perform strongly; vector norm gives an inverse, partial signal, and a single-centroid classifier is near chance.

fits_no_version.finding: In a puzzle text classifier, two label-independent features share one activation direction: food is read by the sign of the projection and country by its magnitude (squared-projection AUC 0.976). A linear probe on country is at chance (0.487) while an MLP probe reaches 0.987.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Networks can store two independent features on one activation direction with different nonlinear readouts, so linear probes miss one of them.

fits_no_version.finding: Gradient-reversal adversarial training makes country linearly unreadable (linear AUC 0.519) while keeping MLP AUC at 0.974. Adding a shape loss raises linear AUC to 0.650.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Adversarial training can make a feature linearly invisible while preserving its nonlinear decodability.

record.problems: The evidence concerns one small text-classifier setup and does not establish how common the effect is. The post reports no uncertainty estimates. It does not test the proposed capacity-pressure cause, and its adversarial experiments deliberately induce the encoding behavior.
record.rows_left_out: The post's experiment accuracy values and the detailed individual entries of the 63 Boolean-combination tests are not included; the aggregate best Boolean match is recorded in r13. The experiment-summary table repeats results recorded for Experiments A and B.

untested.parts: No transformer language-model MLP neurons; no prevalence or layer analysis.
No neuron-level polysemanticity measured. There is no test that more features than dimensions caused the sharing, and 8 features in 64 dimensions gives no evident capacity pressure.
No neuron-level analysis and no manipulation of initialization, regularization or noise.
No comparison of activation function, architecture or regularization.
No canonical polysemantic neurons are revisited.
The readout comparison concerns feature decodability, not how neuron polysemanticity is judged across activation ranges or scoring methods.

record.verdict_notes: All of the record's version links (V3, V6, V7) were removed because the work is at the level of directions and probes, not neurons. The reader's V6 'challenges' label does not hold: V6 concerns canonical neurons with better tools, and none are studied here. The capacity-pressure framing is weakened by the setup itself, with 8 features in a 64-dimensional space. The puzzle model was presumably built by BlueDot to contain a hidden feature, so the encoding may be induced rather than natural; the post says only that it was 'trained the usual way'. r12 and r13 are dataset label analyses, not model results.

versions.untested_parts: No image classifier or vision-model neurons are studied.
The subject is a text classifier, not a transformer language model; no prevalence across MLP neurons, layers, tokens, or contexts is measured.
The post finds two independent labels encoded along the same direction, but does not test whether the network has more features than neurons or whether capacity pressure caused the reuse.
No comparison tests initialization, regularization, or training noise as causes of polysemanticity when capacity is sufficient.
No activation-function, architecture, or regularization comparison tests polysemanticity rates or performance costs.
The post does not revisit canonical vision-model neurons or estimate how frequent unrelated mixtures are across models.
The post compares linear, nonlinear, and geometric readouts, but does not compare explanation-scoring methods or activation-range subsets.

reader_labels.label: supports
reader_labels.reason: Country information is recovered from the squared food-axis projection, and the post reports independent country and food labels sharing that axis (r10-r13); the capacity-pressure mechanism is not established.

reader_labels.label: challenges
reader_labels.reason: The post reports country and food as independent labels while country is encoded on the food direction with a magnitude-based readout, an unrelated mixture in this model (r10-r13).

reader_labels.label: supports
reader_labels.condition: Country on the original classifier's second-layer activations
reader_labels.reason: The linear probe is near chance while the nonlinear and quadratic readouts perform strongly; norm and centroid readouts also differ in effectiveness (r1-r9).
